question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian commercial bank is applying the sources and uses of funds approach to the following month-end forecasts (CAD million). January is the base month. The bank also expects fee income of CAD 14 million in each month.

| Forecast | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Demand deposits | 340 | 325 | 350 | 310 | 330 | 315 |
| Time and savings deposits | 860 | 850 | 905 | 880 | 845 | 870 |
| Commercial loans | 690 | 735 | 700 | 760 | 745 | 720 |
| Consumer loans | 310 | 320 | 335 | 330 | 300 | 325 |

Which month is projected to show the largest liquidity deficit, and how large is it?

options.A: March, a deficit of CAD 100 million
options.B: April, a deficit of CAD 120 million
options.C: April, a deficit of CAD 95 million
options.D: May, a deficit of CAD 60 million

solution:
Largest monthly liquidity deficit from deposit and loan forecasts (CAD).

**Concept and theory**

The sources and uses of funds approach (GARP 5.5) starts from two simple facts: a bank’s liquidity rises when deposits increase and loans decrease, and falls when deposits decrease and loans increase. Deposit growth and loan run-off are sources of liquidity; deposit run-off and loan growth are uses. Whenever sources and uses do not match there is a liquidity gap. When sources exceed uses the gap is positive (a surplus that must be invested quickly); when uses exceed sources the gap is negative (a deficit that must be funded from the cheapest and most timely sources).

question: A member of the board risk committee of an Australian bank asks the CRO how the bank sizes its liquidity reserves on top of the estimates produced by its liquidity estimation models. Which response by the CRO best describes the two components of liquidity reserves?

options.A: The protective component is the reserve called for by the latest forecast, and the planned component is an extra margin set by management’s risk attitude.
options.B: The protective component is fixed by the central bank’s legal reserve rules, so it is identical across all banks holding the same deposits.
options.C: The planned component is the reserve called for by the latest forecast, and the protective component is an extra margin set by management’s risk attitude.
options.D: Once forecasts have been refined, the estimation methods give exact requirements, so the protective component can safely be set to zero.

Planned versus protective components of liquidity reserves (AUD bank).

GARP opens Section 5.5 by noting that each estimation method (sources and uses, structure of funds, liquidity indicators, market signals) “rests on specific assumptions” and yields only an approximation of actual liquidity requirements. That is why a liquidity manager must keep fine-tuning estimates as new information arrives, and why most financial firms build their liquidity reserves in two layers:

| Component | Definition (GARP 5.5) |
|---|---|
| Planned | The reserves called for by the latest forecast |
| Protective | An extra margin of liquid reserves above those dictated by the most recent forecast |

A junior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is setting up the structure of funds approach. She has identified three funding items:

I. SGD 40 million of overnight interbank borrowings that management is sure will run off this period.

III. SGD 600 million of small retail savings balances that rarely move.

Which of the following statements about how she should apply the approach is most accurate?

question: The chief credit officer of a eurozone bank questions why the structure of funds approach adds a loan liquidity requirement equal to 100% of the gap between maximum potential loans and actual loans outstanding. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Borrowers usually leave loan proceeds on deposit at the lender, so only about 30% of the potential new loans needs to be covered by liquid reserves.
options.B: Liquidity takes priority over lending, so the bank should turn down good loan requests whenever its liquid reserves fall below the estimated requirement.
options.C: Borrowers spend loan proceeds at once, yet good loan customers bring deposits and fee business, so the full gap is held in liquid assets or borrowing capacity.
options.D: The full gap must be held as liquid assets on the balance sheet, because unused borrowing capacity cannot count toward a liquidity requirement.

solution:
Why the loan liquidity requirement is 100% of potential minus actual loans (EUR).

**Concept and theory**

The loan side of the structure of funds approach reflects GARP’s view of the lending relationship. A lending institution must be ready at all times to make good loans, meaning loans to customers who meet its quality standards and have legitimate credit needs. It needs liquid reserves for them because, once a loan is made, the borrower spends the proceeds immediately and the funds flow out to other institutions. Yet the lender does not want to turn down any good loan: loan customers bring in new deposits and are normally the principal source of interest and fee earnings. loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese trust bank is preparing an introductory session for newly hired analysts on how the bank classifies future cash flows for liquidity monitoring. The draft slides contain the following statements:

I. Cash flows are classified along two dimensions, time and amount; a cash flow is deterministic in time if it will occur at a future instant that is known with certainty at the reference time.

II. The category of a cash flow is a permanent property of the contract, so it does not change when the point of view is shifted from today to some later reference date.

III. Cash flows whose amount is deterministic are labelled “fixed” in the taxonomy.

IV. A cash flow whose amount is stochastic must also be stochastic in time, since the uncertainty that affects its size also affects its date.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, III and IV only
options.C: I and III only
options.D: II and IV only

solution:
Japanese trust bank slides: which statements about the two dimensions and the deterministic/stochastic labels are correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Chapter 7 by arguing that a clear taxonomy of the cash flows a bank’s business generates is the starting point for any tool that monitors and manages liquidity risk. The taxonomy it proposes uses two dimensions. The first is time: a cash flow is deterministic in time if it will occur at a future instant known with certainty at the reference time (for example, today), and stochastic in time if it can occur at some random future instant. The second is amount: a cash flow is deterministic in amount if its size is known with certainty at the reference time, and stochastic in amount if its size cannot be fully determined.
